kurz: Why the behaviour of the majority is not a reliable signal on the stock exchange, how stories influence prices, what buying near the peak costs in arithmetical terms and which rules protect against it.

bloecke.md:
When choosing between two restaurants in an unfamiliar city, it makes sense to pick the full one. The other diners have already tried the food and so know something you do not. The rule of thumb of doing what others do when in doubt is old, costs nothing and is usually right. On the stock exchange, it does not hold, for a structural reason. The queue outside the restaurant has no influence on the prices on the menu. On the stock exchange, by contrast, the demand of others directly determines the price.

From 1951 onwards, Solomon Asch measured how strongly group pressure works, even when the right answer is obvious. Test subjects were asked to compare the lengths of lines. When tested alone, they were wrong in less than 0.7% of cases. When several fellow participants who were in on the experiment unanimously named the obviously wrong line, the proportion of wrong answers rose to 35.7%. Overall, 74% of the subjects gave in at least once; only 26% stuck to their own perception throughout. And yet the task was simple and the right answer plain to see. On the stock exchange, neither is the case. There, the pressure to conform meets genuine uncertainty, and under these conditions it is at its strongest.

The queue outside a bakery is information, because it arises independently of what you yourself pay. On the stock exchange, everyone who buys because others are buying pushes up the price, and the rising price convinces the next buyer. Information and outcome coincide. Such a feedback loop rests only on itself and on no independent information.

## How information cascades arise

Economics calls the process by which a little information turns into a large movement an [[Information cascade|information cascade]]. Each participant sees the actions of the others but not their reasons. The first two or three act on their own assessment. From the fourth onwards, the observed behaviour of those who went before outweighs their own weak private information, which is therefore no longer used. The result looks like a broad consensus but rests on the judgement of a few. Cascades can therefore trigger strong price movements and are at the same time unstable. A visible counter-signal can reverse them, because there is hardly any substance behind them.

[[André Kostolany]] describes the same process without a model, but with an indicator. He distinguishes between shaky and strong hands (zittrige und hartgesottene Hände). Investors with strong hands have the four Gs that, according to Kostolany, you need on the stock exchange: money, thoughts, patience and luck (Geld, Gedanken, Geduld, Glück). By thoughts he means your own reasoning, that is, understanding what you are buying and why. Investors with shaky hands lack at least one of the first three Gs: money, their own thoughts or patience. Kostolany always looks at the price together with trading volume. If both rise strongly, the securities pass from strong into [[Shaky hands (zittrige Hände)|shaky hands]], and he calls this phase exaggeration. If prices fall on high volume, the shaky hands give up, and a buying zone emerges again.

The formula is often interpreted too broadly. Kostolany meant short-term price formation; for the long term, his own image of the dog on a long lead says the opposite. In the short term, psychology determines the course of prices, in the long term the economy.

bloecke.md:
## Stories as triggers

A cascade needs a trigger, and that is almost always a story. Stories package uncertainty into a plot with a cause, a direction and a protagonist, something tables cannot do. Nassim Taleb calls this the [[Narrative fallacy|narrative fallacy]]. People infer cause and effect from random data because a pattern is easier to remember than a distribution. For investment practice, this means that a convincing story increases the willingness to buy but not the probability of being right, even if both feel the same.

This gives rise to a test. The question is which verifiable figure supports the story, for example revenue growth, margin, market share, interest rate differential, rental yield or another quantity that could prove wrong within twelve months. If no such figure can be found, the story is irrefutable. Such stories accumulate where there is nothing to measure yet: in young companies without profits, in technologies before their first application and in assets without any cash flow. There, the valuation rests entirely on the story.

punkte: It reduces complexity to a memorable sentence
It captures attention and creates a sense of belonging
It makes an investment something you can talk about, even at the dinner table
It explains every price movement seamlessly after the event
It does not increase any probability of occurrence
It says nothing about what is already priced in
It provides neither an entry price nor an upper limit
It does not test counter-arguments; it reinterprets them to suit itself

bloecke.md:
## Social media as an amplifier

Social media accelerate the spread and change the sample that investors get to see; the psychology stays the same. A feed sorts by reactions, not by accuracy. Nuanced posts therefore reach fewer readers than a post showing a doubling. In addition, there is a selection the reader cannot see, because gains are posted and losses are not. The denominator is missing, that is, how many people tried, with what share of their wealth, over what period and against what benchmark. After this filtering, a random distribution looks like a method.

In Germany, the circle of investors has grown. According to the count by the Deutsches Aktieninstitut (German Equity Institute), around 14.1 million people owned shares, equity funds or ETFs in 2025, roughly one in five people aged 14 and over.

How much feeds worsen the returns of individual investors has not been reliably quantified, and percentages on this are estimates. What can be measured is the result across all investors, as the gap between the return of a fund and the return of its investors.

bloecke.md: The direction of the finding is clear; its size is disputed. A 2026 study in the Financial Analysts Journal considers the timing costs measured in this way to be significantly overstated. For this lesson, the pattern is enough. With funds about which there is nothing to tell, investors earn roughly what their fund earns. With funds around which a story is currently circulating, they systematically lose. They are not buying the wrong thing, but they pay in the largest amounts at the wrong time.

bloecke.titel: Price path with three purchases (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: Schematic path over 24 months, not market data. The markers show when and how much money flows in, with little money at the start and the largest part at the peak.

bloecke.titel: Purchases and portfolio value in the model
Price gain of 50%, portfolio loss of 35%
bloecke.md:
After two years, the price stands at 150, that is, 50% above the start. With a lump-sum investment on the first day, the portfolio would be 50% up. The three purchases add up to 43.33 units at an average price of 230.77. With €10,000 paid in, the portfolio value is €6,500, which is minus 35%.

Each individual purchase was understandably justified on its own terms. The mistake lay in how the amounts were spread over time, because 70% of the money flowed in during the month in which the story sounded most convincing. This weighting is the arithmetical cause of every behaviour gap. It also explains why the gap is around 14 points for crypto ETFs and zero for broad large-cap funds.

In January 2021, GameStop rose from around $19 to an intraday high of $483 on 28 January and three weeks later was trading at around $40 again. Bitcoin reached around $69,000 in November 2021 and a year later stood at around $16,000, a fall of about 77%. In Germany, the Neuer Markt (German growth segment) showed the same pattern. The NEMAX All Share lost around 96% from its peak in March 2000 to its low in autumn 2002. The prices are rounded.

A video game retailer, a protocol and a stock exchange segment have nothing in common in substance. The price path nevertheless has the same shape, because it arises from the sequence of story, attention and inflows and not from the object itself.

- The selection is one-sided. You hear about the one who won, while the two who lost stay silent. Your circle of acquaintances is therefore a sample with survivorship bias.
- The reporting format is incomplete. What gets told is the gain in euros, without the return, share of total wealth, period and benchmark. Without these four details, the sentence “I made €4,000” contains no information.
- A tip from a friend creates a social obligation. Checking it and turning it down puts the relationship at risk, so it is checked less carefully.
- Then there is envy. Charlie Munger counts envy among the underestimated motives. The neighbour's return is the worst conceivable yardstick, because it is not risk-adjusted, not complete and not related to your own goal.

Investment advice requires authorisation, namely as an investment service under Section 2(2) WpIG (Investment Firm Act) or Section 1(1a) KWG (Banking Act), alternatively under Section 34f GewO (Trade Regulation Act) for arranging investment funds, and under Section 34h GewO as fee-based advice (Honorarberatung). Anyone who publicly recommends securities is additionally subject to Article 20 of the Market Abuse Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014) and must disclose their own positions and conflicts of interest. Building up a position, promoting it without disclosing this conflict of interest and selling into the purchases this triggers is market manipulation within the meaning of Article 12 MAR. It is prohibited under Article 15 MAR and, as an administrative offence, punishable by a fine under Section 120 WpHG (Securities Trading Act). It is a criminal offence under Section 119 WpHG if it is committed intentionally and thereby influences the price; the attempt is also punishable.

The rules make conflicts of interest visible; they do not prevent bad recommendations. They do not apply to tips in private circles, for example from a brother-in-law at the kitchen table. Such a tip has no legal consequences and is therefore not safeguarded by any of these rules.

## Tax consequences

Jumping on a price rise in the short term requires quick action, and quick action is unfavourable for tax purposes in Germany. Crypto sales within one year are a private disposal transaction (privates Veräußerungsgeschäft) under Section 23(1) sentence 1 no. 2 EStG (Income Tax Act). The gains are taxed at the personal tax rate, not at the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer). The Federal Fiscal Court (BFH) confirmed this in 2023 (IX R 3/22). The €1,000 under Section 23(3) sentence 5 EStG is an exemption threshold (Freigrenze), not an allowance (Freibetrag). If the total gain from private disposal transactions in the calendar year reaches €1,000, the entire gain is taxable. Losses from such transactions can only be offset against gains of the same kind (Section 23(3) sentence 7 EStG).

The same applies to shares. Losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG), not against interest, dividends or fund gains. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG). Investors who buy at the peak and sell at a loss in the downturn end up with a loss pot that can only be offset against future gains of the same kind.

schritte.text: Only buy a security that has stood out in headlines or in your feed in the last 30 days after seven days' distance and with a written justification. Most of these price rises do not last that long.
Record which verifiable figure supports the story and at what value the thesis would be refuted. Without such a figure, no position is opened.
Do not place an order on a day on which you have consumed financial content on social media. The rule relies on separation in time, not on strength of character.

schritte.titel: A cap instead of a ban
schritte.text: Before taking part in a price rise, decide what percentage of the portfolio may be lost completely in the process. A fixed cap holds even under emotional pressure, whereas a mere intention does not.
The benchmark is your own plan and not the return of the acquaintance who talks about it most loudly. Without a written yardstick, you adopt that of the people around you.

bloecke.md: The majority of investors is often right, however. Markets rise most of the time, and investors who reflexively act against the majority make the same mistake with the opposite sign. The point, therefore, is to check whether an opinion is already reflected in the price, not to do the opposite. Caution is called for when three things come together: the justification consists of a story rather than a figure, the number of people involved grows faster than the substance, and the strongest reason to buy is that others have already bought.

mitnehmen: On the stock exchange, the crowd is not an independent source of information, because its purchases themselves form the price, and anyone who follows it merely confirms the signal they are following.
A convincing story increases the willingness to buy but not the probability of being right, and without a verifiable figure it is irrefutable and therefore worthless.
The behaviour gap grows with the attention an investment receives, from 0.0 percentage points for broad large-cap funds to around 14 for crypto ETFs.
A price can rise by 50% while the money paid in loses 35%, because the result depends on the timing and size of the purchases and not on the security bought.
What works are fixed dates and rules such as a waiting period, a numbers test, separating feed and order, and a fixed cap; good intentions alone are not enough.

begriffe.text: A state in which market participants only observe the actions of others and no longer use their own information. A cascade looks like a broad consensus but rests on the judgement of a few and can therefore easily reverse.
The tendency to adopt the behaviour of the majority when uncertain. In Asch's experiments, unanimous group pressure led to 35.7% wrong answers; without the group, the error rate was below 0.7%.
According to Nassim Taleb, the tendency to construct a causal story from random data. It increases the willingness to buy but not the probability of being right.

The fear of missing an opportunity. It is not a cognitive bias in its own right; it arises from the interplay of social proof, envy, recency bias and the urge to act. That is why it is so hard to resist.

Kostolany's term for investors who lack at least one of the first three of his four Gs: money, thoughts or patience. If price and volume rise at the same time, the securities pass from strong into shaky hands.
